t: Maximum Score From Removing Stones - Always Pair the Two Largest Piles
o: Three stone piles hold a, b and c stones; every move removes exactly one stone from each of two different non-empty piles and scores one point, and play ends when fewer than two piles are non-empty. For (2,4,6) you drain pile 1 against pile 3 twice and then pair piles 2 and 3 four times, scoring 6; for (4,4,6) seven moves are possible; for (1,1,1) only one. Two bounds pin down the answer. Every move consumes two stones, so the score cannot exceed floor((a+b+c)/2). Also, if M is the largest pile and T = S - M is what the other two hold together, each move removes either one or two stones from those two piles, so the number of moves is at most T: score <= S - max. Both bounds are simultaneously achievable, giving min(floor(S/2), S - max): for (2,4,6), min(6, 6) = 6; for (4,4,6), min(7, 8) = 7; for (1,1,1), min(1, 2) = 1.
k: Two upper bounds fully determine the answer: floor(S/2) because each move eats two stones, and S - max(a,b,c) because each move claims at most two stones from the union of the two smaller piles.
When the two smaller piles together cannot outweigh the largest (a + b <= c), the answer collapses to exactly a + b.
The greedy rule - always take from the two currently largest piles - provably realizes the bound by keeping the piles balanced.

a.n: Approach 1: Greedy Simulation on the Two Largest
a.i: Mirror the natural strategy: each turn remove one stone from each of the two currently largest piles. With only three piles, a tiny max-heap - or even just re-sorting three numbers - keeps this honest. The simulation runs exactly once per scored point, at most (a+b+c)/2 <= 150000 iterations under these limits, so performance is never a concern. This is also the easiest solution to defend, since its correctness is intuitive even before the bounds are proven.
s: Put the three pile sizes into a max-heap.
Pop the two largest values; if the second is 0, fewer than two non-empty piles remain - stop.
Score one point and push back both values decremented.

c.python:
import heapq

class Solution:
    def maximumScore(self, a: int, b: int, c: int) -> int:
        heap = [-a, -b, -c]
        heapq.heapify(heap)
        score = 0
        while True:
            x = -heapq.heappop(heap)
            y = -heapq.heappop(heap)
            if y == 0:
                break
            score += 1
            heapq.heappush(heap, -(x - 1))
            heapq.heappush(heap, -(y - 1))
        return score

a.t: O(S log 3) = O(S) with S = a + b + c <= 3 * 10^5 - one constant-time heap update per scored point.
a.sp: O(1) - the heap holds three elements.

a.n: Approach 2: Closed Form min(floor(S/2), S - max)
a.i: The two bounds derived above are tight, so skip the simulation entirely: one max and one floor division. If a + b <= c the big pile can only be drained a + b times, and indeed S - M = a + b while 2(a+b) <= S makes a + b the smaller bound; otherwise everything pairs off to floor(S/2), stranding at most one stone when S is odd.
s: Compute S = a + b + c and M = max(a, b, c).

w: State the two bounds before writing any code - they convert a simulation problem into a one-liner, and deriving them is exactly what interviewers reward. If pressed for proof of achievability, describe pairing the largest pile against the smaller ones alternately until a+b <= c, then finishing inside the remaining two piles. Pitfalls: integer division must round down (all quantities are positive, so truncation equals floor); misreading the move as taking two stones from one pile rather than one from each of two different piles; and forgetting that an odd total necessarily strands exactly one stone. Follow-ups: generalize to k piles (the formula min(floor(S/2), S - max) still holds), reconstruct an explicit move sequence, or handle variants where a single move may draw twice from the same pile.
